q: Why are several elevators often grouped around one lobby in larger buildings?
o: So riders wait in one place and cars are dispatched as a group
So each car can have its own separate lobby
So all the cars can share one hoistway door
So the cars can run without any group control
ref: ASME A17.1 elevator and escalator terminology; Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook
n: Grouping lets the controller send whichever car is best. Riders can see all the cars from one spot.

q: Which elevator is sized to carry a patient on a bed or stretcher?
ref: ASME A17.1 elevator and escalator terminology; Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook
n: Bed elevators have deep, narrow cars that fit a bed lengthwise with attendants.

q: Two elevator groups share a lobby: one serves floors 2–10 and the other floors 11–20. What is this called?
ref: ASME A17.1 elevator and escalator terminology; Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook
n: Zoning splits the floors between groups so each car makes fewer stops. The upper group runs express past the lower floors.

q: Which change usually raises the handling capacity of an elevator group?
o: Adding cars or using larger cars
ref: ASME A17.1 elevator and escalator terminology; Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook
n: Handling capacity depends on how many people each car carries and how often cars come.

o: A group of elevators serving the same floors
One elevator serving one floor only
A sump that drains the elevator pit
A group of escalators between two floors
ref: ASME A17.1 elevator and escalator terminology; Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook
n: A bank is dispatched as a group. Big buildings have several banks, each serving a zone.

q: What is a dumbwaiter meant for?
ref: ASME A17.1 elevator and escalator terminology; Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook
n: Dumbwaiters carry food, linen and documents. They are too small for a person to ride in.

q: A 20-storey building has heavy morning up-peak traffic. Which concept cuts stops by giving floor ranges to different groups?
ref: ASME A17.1 elevator and escalator terminology; Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook
n: With zoning, each group serves fewer floors, so round trips are shorter and intervals drop.

q: In elevator traffic analysis, what is the interval?
o: The time for one car to make a full round trip
The average time a passenger rides in a car
The time the doors stay open at each stop
The average time between car departures from the main lobby
ref: ASME A17.1 elevator and escalator terminology; Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook
n: Interval is the round-trip time divided by the number of cars. Offices aim for about 25–30 seconds.

q: What is the round-trip time (RTT) of an elevator?
o: The time for a car to leave the lobby, serve its stops and come back
The average time between car departures from the lobby
The time a passenger waits for a car
The time for the doors to open and close once
ref: ASME A17.1 elevator and escalator terminology; Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook
n: RTT includes travel, stops, door operation and loading. Dividing it by the number of cars gives the interval.

q: Which elevator raises the car by pumping oil into a cylinder under a plunger?
ref: ASME A17.1 elevator and escalator terminology; Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook
n: Hydraulic elevators suit low rises, up to about six floors. They need no overhead machine but use more energy.

q: In a 50-storey building, what is a sky lobby?
o: A roof deck that houses the elevator machine room
A lobby reserved for the freight elevators only
A transfer floor where riders change from shuttles to local cars
A lobby reserved for the fire-service elevator only
ref: ASME A17.1 elevator and escalator terminology; Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook
n: Sky lobbies stack zones on top of each other so local cars in different zones share the same shafts.

q: In elevator planning, what is handling capacity?
o: The rated load of one car, in kilograms
The number of cars in the elevator group
The number of floors the group serves
The share of the population moved in 5 minutes at peak
ref: ASME A17.1 elevator and escalator terminology; Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook
n: Offices typically aim to move 12–15% of their population in five minutes during up-peak.

q: What does 'MRL' mean in elevator terminology?
ref: ASME A17.1 elevator and escalator terminology; Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook
n: MRL means machine-room-less: the drive sits in the hoistway, so no separate machine room is built.

q: Which elevator uses ropes over a driven sheave, with the car balanced by a counterweight?
ref: ASME A17.1 elevator and escalator terminology; Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook
n: Traction elevators suit mid- and high-rise buildings. Friction between ropes and sheave moves the car.

o: Every car stops at every floor in turn
Idle cars are parked at the top floor
Riders key in their floor and are assigned a car
Cars are assigned at random to spread wear
ref: ASME A17.1 elevator and escalator terminology; Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook
n: Grouping riders by destination cuts stops per trip and raises handling capacity.
